lessons.title: How the Three Statements Connect: Following One Transaction Through All Three

children.text: Managers are taught the three statements as three documents. They are not. They are three views of one set of transactions, and they are wired together so tightly that you cannot change a number in one without the other two moving.
This is the lesson that turns everything so far into a single mental model. Once you can follow one transaction through all three, no number in a review meeting can surprise you again.

body.text: There are not three statements. There is one business, photographed from three angles, and the angles are wired together.

children.text: The Three Wires
Only three connections hold the whole structure together. Learn these and the rest is arithmetic.

cells: Profit to equity
Profit for the year in the P&L
Other equity on the balance sheet
Profits the company keeps belong to the owners, so they increase net worth, less any dividend
Cash to cash
Closing cash in the cash flow statement
Cash and cash equivalents on the balance sheet
They are the same number. If they differ, something is wrong
Balance sheet movements to cash flow
Change in receivables, inventory, payables and assets between two balance sheets
Working capital and investing lines in the cash flow statement
The cash flow statement is built by explaining what changed between two balance sheets

body.caption: The first wire, in one line

body.label: The tie-out test
body.value: If the balance sheet does not balance, the model is wrong
body.context: When a finance team builds a three-statement model, the balance sheet balancing is the proof that every transaction has been recorded on both sides. It is not a formatting nicety. It is the only automatic error check the system has.

body.title: Where profit goes
body.textWithBlank: Profit for the year that is not paid out as dividend increases ___ on the balance sheet.
body.explanation: Retained profit accumulates in other equity, principally as retained earnings. This is why a consistently profitable company's net worth grows year after year even if it never issues a single new share.

children.text: Six Transactions, Traced All the Way Through
Here are six routine events at Kesari Foods. Each one is followed across all three statements. Notice how many of them never touch the P&L at all.

body.caption: One transaction at a time (₹ crore)

cells: Sell goods worth 1.0 on 60-day credit, costing 0.52
Revenue +1.0, cost +0.52, profit +0.48
Receivables +1.0, inventory -0.52, equity +0.48
No cash yet. Profit +0.48 is offset by receivables +1.0 and inventory -0.52 in operating
Collect that 1.0 from the distributor
Nothing. The sale was already recorded
Receivables -1.0, cash +1.0
Operating +1.0 as receivables fall
Buy a machine for 3.5, paid in cash
Nothing in the year of purchase
Plant and equipment +3.5, cash -3.5
Investing -3.5
Charge the year's depreciation of 2.0
Depreciation expense 2.0, profit -2.0 before tax
Plant and equipment -2.0, equity down by the post-tax effect
Operating: added back in full, because no cash moved
Draw a term loan of 2.0
Nothing. Borrowing is not income
Borrowings +2.0, cash +2.0
Financing +2.0
Pay a dividend of 1.0
Nothing. Dividends are not an expense
Equity -1.0, cash -1.0
Financing -1.0

body.text: Four of these six never appear in the P&L. Buying a machine, collecting a receivable, taking a loan and paying a dividend are among the largest cash movements a company makes, and a manager watching only the P&L sees none of them. This is precisely why finance refuses to run the business off one statement.

body.title: Which statement is untouched?
body.question: Kesari Foods pays ₹80 lakh to a supplier for flour delivered and recorded last month. Which statement does this payment leave completely unchanged?
body.explanation: The expense was already recorded when the flour was received, so the P&L does not move. The balance sheet changes twice, cash down ₹80 lakh and payables down ₹80 lakh, and the cash flow statement shows the outflow in operating activities through the fall in payables.

children.text: The Question Every Finance Interview Asks
Depreciation increases by ₹10 crore. What happens to all three statements? It sounds like a trick. It is the cleanest possible test of whether you understand the wiring. Assume a 26% tax rate.

body.title: Work it through, one statement at a time

children.text: Start with the P&L, then cash, then the balance sheet. Always in that order.
Profit and loss:
depreciation is an expense, so profit before tax falls by ₹10 crore. Tax falls by 26% of that, which is ₹2.6 crore. Profit after tax falls by ₹7.4 crore.
Cash flow statement:

start from the lower profit after tax of ₹7.4 crore, then add back the full ₹10 crore of depreciation because no cash left the company. Net effect on operating cash is a rise of ₹2.6 crore, which is exactly the tax saved.
Balance sheet:
plant and equipment falls by ₹10 crore. Cash rises by ₹2.6 crore. Equity falls by ₹7.4 crore through lower retained profit.
Check it balances: assets change by minus ₹10 crore plus ₹2.6 crore, which is minus ₹7.4 crore. Equity changes by minus ₹7.4 crore. The two sides move together, so the model holds.
The real insight is the second step. A non-cash charge improves cash, but only by the tax it saves. Anyone who claims depreciation "generates" ₹10 crore of cash has skipped the wiring.

body.title: The cash effect of a non-cash charge
body.prompt: A company records an extra ₹10 crore of depreciation in the year. Its tax rate is 26%. By how much does cash from operations change, in ₹ crore? Enter a positive number for an increase.
body.explanation: Profit after tax falls ₹7.4 crore, then ₹10 crore of depreciation is added back, so operating cash rises ₹2.6 crore. That ₹2.6 crore is the tax saved, which is the only real cash effect of a non-cash charge.

children.text: A Quarter at Kesari Foods, End to End
Four events happen in a single quarter. Opening cash is ₹1.5 crore, opening equity is ₹21 crore. Work out the closing position before reading the answer.
Sales of ₹14 crore, all on credit, with materials and other cash costs of ₹11.5 crore, also on credit and unpaid at quarter end.
Collections from distributors of ₹12 crore, and payments to suppliers of ₹9 crore.
Depreciation of ₹0.5 crore for the quarter.
A fresh term loan of ₹2 crore drawn, and ₹0.4 crore of interest paid.
Profit and loss for the quarter:

Revenue ₹14.0 crore, less cash costs ₹11.5 crore, less depreciation ₹0.5 crore, less interest ₹0.4 crore, gives profit before tax of ₹1.6 crore. Ignoring tax for simplicity, profit for the quarter is ₹1.6 crore.
Cash flow for the quarter:
Operating: collections ₹12.0 crore less supplier payments ₹9.0 crore, which is ₹3.0 crore in.
Financing: loan ₹2.0 crore in, interest ₹0.4 crore out, which is ₹1.6 crore in.
Net change in cash: ₹4.6 crore. Closing cash is ₹1.5 crore plus ₹4.6 crore, which is ₹6.1 crore.
Balance sheet at quarter end, showing only the movements:
Receivables rise by ₹14.0 crore billed less ₹12.0 crore collected, which is ₹2.0 crore.
Payables rise by ₹11.5 crore incurred less ₹9.0 crore paid, which is ₹2.5 crore.
Plant and equipment falls ₹0.5 crore through depreciation. Cash rises ₹4.6 crore. Borrowings rise ₹2.0 crore. Equity rises ₹1.6 crore through profit.

The check: assets move by ₹2.0 crore plus ₹4.6 crore minus ₹0.5 crore, which is ₹6.1 crore. Liabilities and equity move by ₹2.5 crore plus ₹2.0 crore plus ₹1.6 crore, which is ₹6.1 crore. It balances, so the quarter has been recorded correctly.

Read the result: the quarter generated ₹3 crore of operating cash on ₹1.6 crore of profit, because collections ran ahead of billing for once. Cash rose ₹4.6 crore, but ₹2 crore of that was borrowed, not earned.

body.title: What each statement told you about that quarter

columns.label: If you read only the P&L
points: Profit ₹1.6 crore on ₹14 crore of sales
No idea that ₹2 crore of the cash was borrowed

columns.label: If you read all three
points: Operating cash ₹3 crore, ahead of profit
Cash up ₹4.6 crore, of which ₹2 crore is debt
Receivables up ₹2 crore and payables up ₹2.5 crore
Borrowings up, so next quarter carries more interest

body.title: Model the expansion for the CFO
body.scenario: You head operations at Kesari Foods. The CFO asks you to lay out, for the board, what a ₹5 crore packing line funded by a ₹5 crore term loan at 11% does to the three statements over the first two years. The line adds depreciation of ₹0.5 crore a year over ten years and is expected to add ₹1.8 crore of EBITDA a year once it runs at plan, though only half of that in year one during ramp-up.
body.prompt: Set out the effects on each statement for year one and year two.
body.modelAnswer:
Year one, assuming half the benefit:
1. P&L: EBITDA up ₹0.9 crore, less depreciation ₹0.5 crore, less interest ₹0.55 crore, so profit before tax falls about ₹0.15 crore. The first year is dilutive to profit, which the board must hear from you rather than discover later.
2. Cash flow: operating cash up about ₹0.9 crore from the extra EBITDA, before working capital. Investing shows ₹5 crore out in the year the machine is paid for. Financing shows ₹5 crore in from the loan, less interest paid.
3. Balance sheet: plant and equipment up ₹5 crore then down ₹0.5 crore for depreciation, borrowings up ₹5 crore, equity slightly down. Debt to equity moves from 0.62 to about 0.86.
Year two, at full benefit:
4. P&L: EBITDA up ₹1.8 crore, less depreciation ₹0.5 crore, less interest of roughly ₹0.5 crore on a reducing balance, so profit before tax rises about ₹0.8 crore.
5. Cash flow: operating cash up about ₹1.8 crore, investing is now nil for this project, financing shows principal repayment plus interest.
6. Balance sheet: borrowings begin falling as the loan amortises, equity rises with retained profit, and the ratios start recovering.
What to add before the board sees it:
7. The extra working capital the additional volume needs, roughly ₹10 crore of working capital for every ₹50 crore of sales at current ratios, because the loan funds the machine but not the receivables it creates.
8. Interest coverage in year one, which falls from 4.0 towards about 2.9 and should be checked against any covenant.
9. A downside case in which the ramp-up takes four quarters longer, and what that does to coverage.

body.title: Prove the wiring on a real company
steps: Open one company's P&L, balance sheet and cash flow statement for the same year.
Check that closing cash in the cash flow statement equals the cash line on the balance sheet.
Take last year's other equity, add this year's profit, subtract dividends paid, and compare with this year's other equity.
Find depreciation in the P&L and confirm the same figure is added back in the cash flow statement.
Compare the change in trade receivables between the two balance sheets with the receivables line in the cash flow statement.
Note any difference and read the notes, since items such as acquisitions and revaluations explain most gaps.

cards.definition: Profit for the year, less dividends, increases other equity on the balance sheet.
Closing cash in the cash flow statement is the same number as cash on the balance sheet.
The cash flow statement is built by explaining what changed between two consecutive balance sheets.
An expense such as depreciation that reduces profit without moving cash, and whose only cash effect is the tax it saves.
A linked financial model in which the balance sheet balancing proves every entry was recorded twice.
Checking that figures agree across statements, the standard first test of whether numbers can be trusted.

points: The three statements are three views of one business, connected by three wires.
Profit less dividends flows into equity, closing cash equals balance sheet cash, and balance sheet movements build the cash flow statement.
Many of the largest cash events, including capital expenditure, collections, borrowing and dividends, never appear in the P&L.
An extra ₹10 crore of depreciation lowers profit after tax by ₹7.4 crore and raises operating cash by ₹2.6 crore, which is simply the tax saved.
If the balance sheet does not balance, the numbers are wrong. It is the only built-in error check.
When you model a decision, state its effect on all three statements, and on the ratios the lenders watch.

body.text: Kesari Foods is fictional and all figures are constructed for teaching, with tax ignored in the quarterly example to keep the arithmetic visible. Nothing here is investment advice.
